# Sela Sutta (Snp 3.7 (PTS Snp 102))

**ID:** Snp 3.7 (PTS Snp 102)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Sela Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sela Sutta* (Snp 3.7; PTS Snp 102) is a mixed prose-and-verse discourse belonging to the *Mahāvagga* of the *Suttanipāta* [Norman 1983; Winternitz 1933]. The narrative relates the encounter between the Buddha and the brāhmaṇa Sela, who approaches to ascertain whether the Buddha possesses the thirty-two physical marks of a great man (*mahāpurisa*) [Norman 1983]. Because two of these marks are hidden, the Buddha exercises supernormal powers to reveal his broad tongue and sheath-encased organ to Sela [Norman 1983; Anālayo 2017]. Impressed by these signs, Sela recites verses of praise and urges the Buddha to rule mankind as a "king of kings" (*rājābhirāja*); the Buddha responds by affirming his status as a spiritual king who turns the wheel of the Dhamma [Endo 1997]. Convinced, Sela and his assembly of students take ordination and subsequently attain arahantship [Anālayo 2017].

The text is identical in content to *Majjhima Nikāya* 92 (*Sela Sutta*), and its verse portion is preserved independently in the *Theragāthā* (Thag 16.6, *Selattheragāthā*) [Norman 1983]. Its opening narrative concerning the ascetic Keṇiya parallels the Vinaya *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* (Kd 6), which scholars note presents a shorter version lacking the Sela episode [Katre 1931]. Outside Pali, a parallel appears in the Chinese *Ekottarika-āgama* (EA 49.6) as well as the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu*, with related passages in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya (*Bhaiṣajyavastu* and *Saṅghabhedavastu*) [Anālayo 2017]. Northern sources, such as the *Divyāvadāna*, cite the *Sailagāthā* alongside the *Arthavarga* and *Munigāthā* as a recognized early scriptural text [Hazra 1994; Lamotte 1988].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: MN 92 (PTS MN ii 146) Sela Sutta
- Passage-level parallels: Lzh Dg Kd 7 Bhesajja Khandhaka; Kd 6 Bhesajjakkhandhaka; EA 49.6; Thag 16.6 Selattheragāthā; Snp 3.6 (PTS Snp 91) Sabhiya Sutta; San Lo Mvu 108 The Three Kāśyapas
- Resembling parallels: SF 12; Iti 100 (It 4.1 PTS It 101) Brāhmaṇadhammayāga Sutta
- Mentioned in: Mil 5.3.10 Vaṇṇabhaṇanapañha; Mil 5.5.8 Brāhmaṇarājavādapañha

**Sources**

- [Norman 1983] K. R. Norman, Pali Literature (1983) — Narrative summary of Sela examining the 32 marks, supernormal revelation of hidden marks, and correspondence to MN 92 and Thag 16.6.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, History of Indian Literature, Vol. II (1933) — Discussion of the relationship between Snp 3.7 and the Majjhima Nikāya.
- [Endo 1997] Toshiichi Endo, Buddha in Theravada Buddhism (1997) — Discussion of Sela inviting the Buddha to be 'king of kings' (rājābhirāja) and its canonical occurrences.
- [Anālayo 2017] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Buddhapada and the Bodhisattva Path (2017) — Details on the 32 marks, the tongue and sheath-encased organ, ordination of Sela's students, and the Ekottarika-āgama parallel.
- [Katre 1931] S. M. Katre, Early Buddhist Ballads and Their Relation to Older Upanishadic Literature (1931) — Analysis of the Keṇiya narrative and comparison with the Vinaya account.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Citation of the Sailagāthā in the Divyāvadāna alongside the Arthavarga and Munigāthā.
- [Lamotte 1988] Étienne Lamotte, History of Indian Buddhism (1988) — Identification of the Sailagāthā among Northern Sanskrit Kṣudraka texts corresponding to Selasutta.
